passage:
For much of the nineteenth century, the music of Johann Sebastian Bach was regarded primarily as the work of a learned craftsman rather than that of a great composer. Concertgoers who thrilled to Beethoven or wept at Schubert tended to speak of Bach with respect, but the respect was of the sort one offers to a teacher of harmony: he had, it was said, mastered the rules, but he had not, like the Romantics, expressed himself through them. This standard view persisted well into the early twentieth century, and it still echoes whenever Bach is described as a composer of the head rather than of the heart.

The view captures something real. Bach did devote unusual attention to technical problems, and many of his works were plainly written for instruction, including pieces he composed to help his own children learn the keyboard. But to leave the matter there is to mistake a composer's discipline for his final aim. A closer acquaintance with the music shows that Bach's technical ingenuity was almost always in the service of expressive ends. The unfolding of a fugue, which can look on the page like an exercise in pattern, functions in performance as a way of gradually disclosing a single musical idea from many angles, and the listener who follows its progress is led through something closer to an argument than to a puzzle.

The misreading of Bach as a pure craftsman has its roots in the changing place of instrumental music in the nineteenth century. For Beethoven's heirs, instrumental music was the privileged vehicle for the artist's inner life, and a composer who did not supply obvious emotional signals — sudden dynamic contrasts, yearning melodies, programmatic titles — was assumed to lack such a life. Bach, whose emotional signals are often embedded in the movement of inner voices rather than placed on the musical surface, did not announce himself in the expected ways, and listeners concluded that he had little to announce.

Yet a sympathetic ear, trained to follow several independent melodic lines at once, will find in Bach's cantatas and instrumental works an emotional range that compares favorably with that of any later composer. The pieces do not weep on cue, but they grieve, exult, reflect, and console, often in the space of a few minutes. What the nineteenth-century listener heard as coolness was in fact a particular kind of restraint, one that trusted the music's architecture to carry feeling without underlining it. Seen this way, Bach is not the craftsman of legend, nor a closet Romantic, but a composer whose expressive aims pass through his technical means rather than around them.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The view of Bach as a merely technical composer misses the fact that his technical devices serve expressive ends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bach's reputation in the nineteenth century suffered because audiences of that era preferred Beethoven and Schubert.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bach should properly be regarded as an early Romantic composer whose emotional aims were simply misunderstood.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Understanding Bach's fugues requires a listener capable of following several independent melodic lines simultaneously.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Much of Bach's keyboard music was written for instructional purposes, including the training of his own children.

explanations.correct: The passage sets up the standard 'craftsman, not composer' view in paragraph 1 and devotes the remainder to showing that Bach's technical ingenuity is in the service of expressive aims. A captures both the view being corrected and the author's corrective.
explanations.B: Paragraph-restatement-not-main-point: captures a contextual observation, not the thesis about the relation between technique and expression.
explanations.C: Too-strong / opposite-of-author: the final paragraph explicitly denies that Bach is 'a closet Romantic.'
explanations.D: Too narrow: the ability to follow independent lines is mentioned once to support the thesis, not as the thesis.
explanations.E: Half-right / paragraph-restatement: true per paragraph 2 but leaves out the corrective move that defines the passage.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the nineteenth-century view of Bach as a craftsman rather than a composer can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: complete rejection as based on factual error

choices.label: B
choices.text: partial agreement combined with a judgment that the view is ultimately inadequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, qualified only by minor reservations

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the view has little bearing on contemporary concerns

choices.label: E
choices.text: uncertainty about whether the view has any defensible content at all

explanations.correct: The author writes that the standard view 'captures something real' (paragraph 2) — Bach did devote unusual attention to technical problems — but argues that it 'mistakes a composer's discipline for his final aim.' That is exactly partial agreement plus a judgment of inadequacy.
explanations.A: Too-strong: the author explicitly concedes that the view captures something real.
explanations.C: Opposite-tone: the author is critical of the view overall, not endorsing it.
explanations.D: The author engages with the view at length; indifference is unsupported.
explanations.E: Opposite of the text: the author clearly identifies what the view gets right.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longstanding view is stated, partly conceded, explained historically, and then revised.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing scholarly theories are presented, and one is shown to be false.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A composer's career is traced chronologically from early instruction pieces to mature works.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An interpretive principle is introduced and then applied to a sequence of unrelated cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critical consensus is described, defended against recent attacks, and reaffirmed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 states the traditional view; paragraph 2 concedes what it gets right and begins the correction; paragraph 3 explains historically why the view arose; paragraph 4 offers the author's revised reading.
explanations.B: Mis-sequencing: the passage is not structured as a head-to-head between two theories, and neither is shown to be 'false.'
explanations.C: No chronology of Bach's career is traced.
explanations.D: Plausible-but-unused: no single interpretive principle is applied to multiple cases.
explanations.E: Opposite-tone: the consensus is being revised, not reaffirmed.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the nineteenth-century assumption that Bach lacked an inner life rested principally on

choices.label: A
choices.text: the fact that Bach composed primarily for religious rather than concert settings

choices.label: B
choices.text: the absence in his music of the obvious emotional signals that later audiences had come to expect

choices.label: C
choices.text: the widespread belief that fugues are exercises in pattern rather than arguments

choices.label: D
choices.text: a general nineteenth-century preference for vocal music over instrumental works

choices.label: E
choices.text: a lack of documentary evidence concerning the composer's private correspondence

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that a composer who did not supply 'obvious emotional signals — sudden dynamic contrasts, yearning melodies, programmatic titles — was assumed to lack such a life,' and that Bach's signals did not announce themselves in the expected ways.
explanations.A: Plausible-world fact not stated: the passage never discusses religious versus concert settings.
explanations.C: Wrong sentence: the fugue-as-pattern framing appears in paragraph 2 as a misreading of the music, not as the basis for the assumption about Bach's inner life.
explanations.D: Outside scope: the passage discusses instrumental music's prestige but never a preference for vocal music.
explanations.E: Outside scope: private correspondence is never mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's remark in paragraph 2 that a fugue 'functions in performance as a way of gradually disclosing a single musical idea from many angles' serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate how Bach's technical devices carry out expressive aims

choices.label: B
choices.text: concede that Bach's fugues are more difficult to follow than his other works

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that fugues should be studied from the score rather than heard in performance

choices.label: D
choices.text: compare Bach's fugues unfavorably with the emotional directness of Romantic works

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that Bach's fugues were composed primarily as instructional exercises

explanations.correct: The remark appears as the author's concrete example of the claim immediately above — that Bach's technical ingenuity 'was almost always in the service of expressive ends.' Its function is illustrative.
explanations.B: Accurate-sounding but wrong function: the passage never grades fugues by difficulty of following.
explanations.C: Opposite of the text: the remark appeals to what happens 'in performance.'
explanations.D: Wrong function / opposite-tone: the remark is used to defend Bach, not to rank him below Romantics.
explanations.E: Function from a different paragraph: instructional composition is mentioned in paragraph 2, but not as the point of this particular sentence.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A composer's emotional range cannot be judged fairly on the basis of surface features alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any composer whose music lacks programmatic titles should be classified as a formalist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bach's keyboard works are more emotionally expressive than his cantatas.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Instrumental music became the central artistic medium only after Bach's lifetime had ended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nineteenth-century listeners were incapable of recognizing musical emotion in any form.

explanations.correct: The author argues that Bach's emotional signals are embedded in inner voices rather than placed on the surface, and that listeners who judged by surface signals missed his range. That directly supports A.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the author uses programmatic titles as an example of surface signals, not as a criterion for classifying composers.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage treats cantatas and instrumental works together and does not compare them.
explanations.D: Half-right: the passage discusses the rise of instrumental music in the nineteenth century but does not fix a moment relative to Bach's life.
explanations.E: Overreach: the author criticizes a misreading, not a general incapacity.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the interpretive pattern the author applies to Bach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist once dismissed as merely ornamental is reappraised when readers notice that her elaborate sentences carry precise emotional content.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A painter long celebrated for technical skill falls out of fashion when a new generation prefers more austere styles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A poet's private letters are published, allowing scholars to confirm biographical speculations that had long circulated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A philosopher abandons an early technical vocabulary in favor of a plainer style accessible to general readers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A composer widely regarded as emotionally expressive is shown, on close analysis, to have relied heavily on formal conventions.

explanations.correct: The pattern is: an artist dismissed as technically accomplished but expressively empty is shown, on closer attention, to use technical devices as the very vehicle of expression. A mirrors this exactly.
explanations.B: Surface-similarity: involves fashion and technical skill but reverses the direction — the artist falls out of favor rather than being reappraised upward.
explanations.C: Wrong mechanism: the pattern concerns the relation of technique to expression, not the emergence of new biographical evidence.
explanations.D: Wrong mechanism: the pattern does not involve a change in the artist's own style.
explanations.E: Inverts the direction: this is the opposite move — reducing an expressive artist to formalism.

passage:
In the study of traditional tales, the figure known as the trickster — a clever, unruly character who outwits stronger beings by guile — has long posed a puzzle for interpreters. Anansi the spider in West African tradition, Coyote in many Native American traditions, and Hermes in early Greek mythology are all commonly grouped together under this label, and the grouping has encouraged a familiar reading: the trickster, it is said, exists to entertain, and his escapades serve chiefly as comic relief from the more solemn concerns of myth. This reading is not wrong, but it is partial, and taken alone it misses what makes the figure so persistent across cultures.

To see why, consider that the trickster's victories almost always depend on his marginal position. He is smaller than his opponents, lower in the social order, or denied access to the ordinary means of getting what he wants. His tools are speech, disguise, and an eye for rules that others follow without thinking. When Anansi secures the world's stories from the sky god, or when Coyote obtains fire from beings who hoarded it, the audience laughs, but it also absorbs a lesson about how the weak can act on a world arranged for the strong. The humor, in other words, is the vehicle of something more serious, and removing the seriousness leaves only a thin residue of jokes.

A second common reading treats the trickster as a symbol of pure disorder, a figure whose appeal lies in his willingness to break every rule. This too captures a real feature of the stories: trickster tales are full of taboo violations and reversals of expectation. But the trickster does not simply destroy the order he confronts. Often, as in the fire-theft stories, his transgressions bring a benefit that the community eventually accepts as its own. The order that results is not the order that existed before, but neither is it chaos; it is an order that has been forced to make room for something previously excluded.

Seen together, these observations suggest that the trickster's cross-cultural appeal rests on neither his comic charm nor his disruptive energy, but on the way he dramatizes a problem that every tradition faces: how to acknowledge, from within its own stories, that the settled order is not the whole of what is possible. The trickster does not merely amuse, and he does not merely rebel. He holds open a small, licensed space in which the rules can be examined from outside without being abandoned, and that, rather than his cleverness, is what keeps him at home in so many different mythologies.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The trickster figure is compelling across cultures because he gives traditions a way to reflect on their own settled order without discarding it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The trickster figure is best understood as a symbol of pure disorder whose appeal lies in his willingness to break rules.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anansi, Coyote, and Hermes should not be classified together, since each arises from a distinct cultural context.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The humor in trickster tales is the principal reason these stories have been preserved across so many traditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trickster tales function mainly to teach listeners specific lessons about how the weak can prevail over the strong.

explanations.correct: Paragraphs 2 and 3 qualify the 'comic relief' and 'pure disorder' readings, and paragraph 4 states the author's integrating thesis: the trickster holds open a licensed space in which a tradition examines its own rules. A captures that thesis.
explanations.B: Opposite-of-author: paragraph 3 explicitly rejects the 'pure disorder' reading as partial.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage accepts the grouping and uses it productively.
explanations.D: Paragraph-restatement-not-main-point: captures the first reading the author corrects, not the thesis.
explanations.E: Too narrow: the weak-versus-strong theme is one strand, subsumed by the larger claim about reflection on order.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the view that the trickster exists mainly to provide comic relief is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissal of the view as a misreading produced by careless scholarship

choices.label: B
choices.text: acceptance of the view as capturing something real but not the whole of what matters

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, with only a single minor qualification

choices.label: D
choices.text: suspicion that the view has no defensible content and is merely conventional

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutrality, since the author considers the question ultimately unanswerable

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 concedes that the comic-relief reading 'is not wrong, but it is partial.' That is precisely acceptance-with-qualification.
explanations.A: Too-strong: the author explicitly allows that the reading captures something real.
explanations.C: Opposite-tone: the author is corrective rather than endorsing.
explanations.D: Too-strong in the other direction; the author credits the view with capturing a real feature.
explanations.E: The author is not neutral; a clear qualifying judgment is offered.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the trickster's victories almost always depend on

choices.label: A
choices.text: his unusual physical strength relative to his opponents

choices.label: B
choices.text: the direct assistance of more powerful mythological beings

choices.label: C
choices.text: his marginal position and his skill with speech, disguise, and rules

choices.label: D
choices.text: the willingness of his community to abandon its ordinary customs

choices.label: E
choices.text: the intervention of a divine authority that sanctions his rule-breaking

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that the trickster's victories 'almost always depend on his marginal position' and identifies his tools as 'speech, disguise, and an eye for rules that others follow without thinking.'
explanations.A: Altered qualifier / opposite: the passage specifies that he is smaller or lower in the social order.
explanations.B: Plausible world-fact not stated: the passage does not mention assistance from more powerful beings.
explanations.D: Wrong sentence: the passage says the community eventually accepts the benefit, not that it abandons its customs.
explanations.E: Outside scope: divine sanction is not mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of fire-theft stories in paragraph 3 functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: show that the trickster's transgressions can produce benefits the community comes to accept

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that Coyote tales are more sophisticated than other trickster traditions

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish the historical priority of Native American trickster tales over West African ones

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the comic dimension of trickster tales noted in paragraph 1

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that taboo violations in trickster tales are usually punished

explanations.correct: The fire-theft example is introduced to show that the trickster's rule-breaking 'brings a benefit that the community eventually accepts as its own,' supporting the author's correction of the 'pure disorder' reading.
explanations.B: Outside scope: the passage does not rank traditions by sophistication.
explanations.C: Outside scope: no claim of historical priority is made.
explanations.D: Function from a different paragraph: the comic dimension is a paragraph-1 concern; in paragraph 3 the example serves the order/disorder discussion.
explanations.E: Opposite of text: the example shows benefit, not punishment.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a story in which a trickster figure broke every rule of his society and left no lasting change behind would

choices.label: A
choices.text: confirm the author's view that the trickster represents pure disorder

choices.label: B
choices.text: fit less comfortably than usual with the author's account of trickster tales

choices.label: C
choices.text: be unintelligible to audiences outside the tradition in which it was first told

choices.label: D
choices.text: prove that the comic-relief reading of trickster tales is entirely mistaken

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that trickster tales and myths of creation share a common origin

explanations.correct: The author argues that trickster tales typically leave a changed order behind — transgression plus accepted benefit. A tale that broke every rule without lasting change would be a poor fit for that account.
explanations.A: Opposite-of-author: the author rejects the 'pure disorder' reading.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage makes no claim about cross-cultural intelligibility.
explanations.D: Too-strong: the author treats the comic-relief reading as partial, not entirely mistaken.
explanations.E: Outside scope: creation myths are not discussed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's position that the trickster holds open a licensed space for examining settled order?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In many traditions, trickster tales were performed during festivals in which ordinary social roles were temporarily suspended.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trickster figures in some traditions are depicted as physically small or animal in form.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some scholars have argued that Anansi tales originated before Coyote tales.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Audiences typically laugh at the moment in a trickster tale when the trickster is first outwitted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain trickster tales survive only in fragments, making their endings difficult to reconstruct.

explanations.correct: If trickster tales were performed in festivals that formally suspended ordinary roles, that confirms the author's picture of a 'small, licensed space' in which the settled order can be examined from outside without being abandoned.
explanations.B: Off-target claim: supports the 'marginal position' observation from paragraph 2, not the licensed-space thesis of paragraph 4.
explanations.C: Outside scope: historical priority does not bear on the author's claim.
explanations.D: Wrong direction / off-target: a moment of laughter does not specifically support the licensed-examination claim.
explanations.E: Outside scope: survival of fragments does not speak to the function the author ascribes.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the role the author assigns to the trickster figure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A traditional legal system designates a ceremonial role, filled during an annual assembly, whose holder is permitted to voice complaints that other members of the community cannot.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A group of rebels overturns the government of their country and replaces its laws with entirely new ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historian writes a comic biography of a political leader, drawing attention to the leader's personal eccentricities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A theater troupe entertains audiences with purely slapstick performances that avoid political subjects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A student masters the rules of a game so thoroughly that she never violates them in competition.

explanations.correct: The trickster holds open a small, licensed space in which rules can be examined from outside without being abandoned. A ceremonial role that licenses otherwise-unpermitted complaints within a standing legal order mirrors this precisely.
explanations.B: Inverts the direction: the trickster does not overturn the order; he opens a space within it.
explanations.C: Surface-similarity: involves humor but lacks the licensed examination of shared rules; the biography addresses one individual's eccentricities.
explanations.D: Matches only the comic-relief strand the author treats as partial; no reflection on order.
explanations.E: Opposite of the pattern: the student never steps outside the rules.
